tour.title: Fortezza, Harbour & the Old Lanes
tour.summary: A short, flat walk through the best-preserved Venetian town on Crete — harbour and Egyptian lighthouse, a Renaissance fountain and meeting house, a church that became a mosque and then a music school, the great Fortezza on its hill, and the last surviving city gate.
tour.overviewText:
Rethymno is the Cretan town that looks most Italian and is proudest of being Greek. Its old town — the palia poli, the old city — was laid out almost entirely under the Republic of Venice, which ruled Crete from the thirteenth century until 1669, and it survived because nothing since has had the money or the will to flatten it. The result is a knot of arched doorways, stone staircases and carved facades that could pass for a small Lombard town, wrapped around a Venetian harbour and a hilltop fortress. Rethymno was never the island's capital; it was the useful middle stop between Heraklion and Chania, and it grew rich as a harbour town, shipping out olive oil, wine and cheese from the Cretan hills.

Three empires made what you will walk through. The Venetians gave the town its shape: walls in the 1540s, a harbour, civic buildings modelled on Venice itself. The Ottomans took it in 1646 and stayed more than 250 years, turning churches into mosques and adding minarets, wooden balconies and fountain domes; their people were mostly Cretans who had converted to Islam, Greek-speaking and Cretan-born, not settlers shipped in from Anatolia. Then in 1923 Greece and Turkey agreed to exchange their religious minorities, and the last Muslims of Crete left — which is why the town's minarets now stand on a music school and a museum rather than on working mosques. In between came the Cretan Renaissance, a brief, brilliant flowering of Greek literature and painting under Venetian rule: the epic romance Erotokritos, written around 1600 by Vitsentzos Kornaros in the Cretan dialect, is still recited here, and the painter El Greco trained on this island.

This is also resistance country. Twenty-three kilometres inland, the monastery of Arkadi became a national symbol in November 1866, when besieged Cretans blew up their own gunpowder rather than surrender to Ottoman troops — an act that turned European opinion toward Cretan independence. You will not visit it on this walk, but its memory is in the street names and in the air.

The walk is short and mostly flat. It begins at the Venetian harbour and its lighthouse, threads into the old lanes for the Rimondi Fountain and the Venetian Loggia, crosses to the church-turned-mosque-turned-music-school at Neratze, climbs the hill to the Fortezza, and finishes in the lanes by the old city gate, the Porta Guora. Nothing is more than a few minutes from anything else.

Everything is priced in euros (€), the currency Greece has used since 2002. Comfortable shoes matter: the lanes are cobbled, and the fortress interior is rough underfoot. September evenings are warm and the town eats late, so an afternoon start lets you finish over dinner on the water. If Santorini is next, a seasonal fast catamaran runs from Rethymno's port straight to Santorini in about two and a quarter hours, from May to October, roughly twice a week and from about €104 — check it is running, because the plan B is a bus to Heraklion (about an hour and a half) and a ferry from there.

So start at the water, and let the town pull you inland.
tour.difficulty: Easy. Flat, shaded lanes in the old town, and one real climb — the cobbled ramp up to the Fortezza. The whole route is under two kilometres of walking, but the lanes are narrow, cobbled and uneven, and the fortress interior is rough ground.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start in the mid-afternoon, early enough that the Fortezza is open and late enough to reach its walls in the golden light, then let the last stretch and dinner fall after sunset, when the harbour and lanes come alive. In September the worst heat has eased by late afternoon; mornings are quieter and cooler, but the fortress and the lanes look better in the softer evening light.

stops.name: Venetian Harbour & Lighthouse
stops.narration:
Start where the town does, at the water. This little bay is the reason Rethymno exists: a natural harbour on the north coast of Crete, sheltered from the prevailing wind and sitting halfway between the island's two bigger cities. The Venetians — the merchant republic of Venice, which took Crete in the early thirteenth century — saw the obvious commercial gap and built a working port here, making Rethymno the island's third city after Heraklion, which they called Candia, and Chania, which they called Canea. The harbour was never large enough for the great war galleys, but it was perfect for the smaller trade that paid for the town: olive oil, wine, cheese and honey coming down from the hills, and imported cloth, metal and sugar going back up.

Notice the town's plan while you look at it. Rethymno's main street, the Ruga Maistra — the Venetian name for a street — runs parallel to the shore, and the lanes step back from it one behind another. That is unusual for Crete. Heraklion and Chania turned their backs on the sea for defence; Rethymno faced it, because here the sea was the business.

Now the lighthouse at the end of the mole. It is not Venetian, despite the setting. In the 1830s Crete was run by Egypt — nominally still part of the Ottoman Empire, but governed by the dynasty of Muhammad Ali, an Ottoman commander in Egypt whose family had been called in to crush a Greek uprising and then stayed — and it was Egyptian engineers who rebuilt this tower on the old Venetian sea wall. It is the second-largest surviving Egyptian lighthouse in Crete, after the one at Chania. The whitewashed base and the tower above it are what most photographs of Rethymno are really of.

The economics have turned over completely. The barrels and the warehouses are gone; the waterfront now sells dinner, boat trips and sunsets, and the fishing boats that still work out of here land mostly for the tavernas beside them. Tourism is the town's income now, along with the olive oil and cheese that still leave from the surrounding hills. Which means you are part of the trade — order something later and you are, quite literally, what the harbour catches.

There is no ticket here: the harbour is public ground at all hours. The quay is level and easy, but the breakwater out to the lighthouse is rough stone, can be slippery, and is closed in rough weather. Judge it yourself. Then walk up into the lanes towards the fountain.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. The harbour and quay are open public ground at all hours. The breakwater can be closed in high winds — verify on the day.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Best in late afternoon and at dusk, when the light on the water is at its best and the tavernas are setting out their tables.
stops.accessibility: The quay is flat and step-free. The breakwater out to the lighthouse is rough, uneven stone with no handrail and is sometimes closed in bad weather — not suitable for wheelchairs or unsteady walkers.
stops.insiderTip: Walk out along the mole early if you want the lighthouse to yourself; by evening it fills with people photographing the sunset. Either way, look back at the town from the end of the breakwater — the Fortezza on its hill above the old roofs is the shot.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the harbour and walk south into the old town, following the signs and the crowds towards the centre. After about five minutes of lanes you reach Platanos Square and the carved stone wall of the Rimondi Fountain — our next stop, in the middle of the old town.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Pjotr Mahhonin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Rimondi Fountain
stops.narration:
This is the town's oldest working piece of plumbing, and it is also a piece of civic showing-off. The Rimondi Fountain was built in 1626 by Alvise Rimondi, the Venetian Rector — the governor Venice sent out to run Rethymno — and it replaced an older, rain-damaged fountain on the same spot. The problem it solved was real. Rethymno's population had grown through the sixteenth century, and the town's wells and cisterns could no longer keep up; water was scarce and sometimes bad. Rimondi repaired the old aqueduct that brought water from a spring in the hills south-east of town and paid for the new fountain largely out of his own pocket. The Latin inscription still legible on the architrave reads LIBERALITATIS FONTES — roughly, 'fountains of generosity' — and the Rimondi coat of arms, the family emblem, sits above the central basin. A governor who wanted to be remembered, and got his wish.

Read it like an architect. Four fluted columns rise from basins, with Ionic-style bases and Corinthian capitals — the ornate, leaf-carved tops of columns — cut from local Alfa limestone, a soft, pale stone that is easy to carve and hardens in the air. Three carved heads, usually described as lions, spout water into three troughs, which were probably for watering animals. The whole thing is composed like the facade of a Roman building, and it copies pattern books that were circulating in Renaissance Italy, above all the work of the architect Sebastiano Serlio. But look at the proportions: they are heavy rather than elegant, and that is a clue. The fountain was most likely carved by Cretan masons, not imported Italian ones. Crete had its own trained stone-carvers, and under Venetian rule they learned to speak the Renaissance in a Cretan accent.

The Ottomans kept the fountain and improved its setting. They built a domed canopy over it, carried on arches, so people could draw water out of the sun; it was known then as the Great Fountain. Only the stub of one supporting pier survives today; the rest of the dome is gone. And one darker detail sits beside the pleasure of the square. The plane tree that gives Platanos Square its name — platani is Greek for plane tree — was, under Ottoman rule, where condemned men were hanged. Public water and public execution, a few metres apart. Towns are like that.

It is free and public, running day and night. The water is generally fine, but if you are cautious, as many locals are, fill your bottle from a café instead. The Loggia, the next stop, is barely a minute's walk away.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. It is a public fountain on an open square, running day and night.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. The square is liveliest in the evening, when the surrounding cafés and bars fill up.
stops.accessibility: Level paved square, step-free. The fountain is viewed from the flat square in front of it.
stops.insiderTip: Find the carved Rimondi coat of arms above the middle basin and the word LIBERALITATIS on the architrave. Then notice how heavy the columns look for supposedly Italian work — the giveaway that this was carved by Cretan masons.
stops.nextStopDirections: Turn back east along the lane for a minute or two, towards the harbour side of the old town, and you reach the Loggia — the square, arched building of pale stone, its three arched fronts facing the lane.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Uoaei1, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: The Venetian Loggia
stops.narration:
This plain, handsome, square building is one of the clearest statements of how Venice ran a colony. A loggia — the word is Italian — is a covered gallery, open on one or more sides, a kind of roofed porch. Venice had a famous one on St Mark's Square, and the towns it ruled copied it. This is Rethymno's, built in the sixteenth century, possibly to a design by Michele Sanmicheli, the Veronese military engineer who also drew up the city's walls. Originally it stood open at the front under a wooden roof; in 1625 an upper storey was added, giving it the two-level look you see now. It is the best-preserved building of its kind on Crete.

What happened here was government, not prayer. The Loggia was the meeting place of the Venetian nobility and officials of Rethymno — a club, a chamber of commerce and a town hall rolled into one, where the town's leading men discussed trade, taxes and politics, and where deals were struck and reputations made. Venice ruled through a small resident elite: a Rector at the top, sent out from Venice for a fixed term, a council of nobles beneath him, and a Cretan population that was taxed, recruited for labour and, for a long time, kept out of the room. That is the honest reading of a beautiful building. The grandeur of Venetian Rethymno was built by, and largely for, a narrow class.

Then the layers pile up, as they do everywhere in this town. After the Ottomans took Rethymno in 1646, the Loggia was converted into a mosque, and a minaret — the tower from which a muezzin calls Muslims to prayer — went up on its west side. That minaret was pulled down in the 1930s, so the building has come full circle back to something like its original shape. Today it belongs to the Greek Ministry of Culture: the Archaeological Receipts Fund, a government office that sells guidebooks and plaster casts of sculptures from sites across Greece.

So you will most likely see it from the outside, which is enough. Walk round all three arched sides and notice how well the stone has lasted — this is what a Renaissance town looked like when it was working, with its fountain for the body and its loggia for the business of the city. Next, the church that became a mosque and then a music school.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to view from the street. The interior is a working government office, so it is not open as a sight; step in only if the door is open to the public.
stops.openingHours: The exterior is visible at all hours. The building itself is a Ministry of Culture office and keeps office hours on working days.
stops.accessibility: Level lane and square in front, step-free. The building's interior is not a visitor route.
stops.insiderTip: Walk round all three arched sides rather than just the front — the Loggia was designed to be seen in the round, and the side arches are the least photographed part. Look for where the Ottoman minaret once stood on the west side.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the Loggia, head south-west through the lanes towards the tall minaret rising above the rooftops. It is a few minutes' walk to the Neratze Mosque, in the small square called Mikrasiaton.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: C messier, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Neratze Mosque
stops.narration:
You are looking at a building that has been three things in four hundred years, and each layer is still visible if you know where to look. It began as the church and monastery of Santa Maria, run by Augustinian friars — a Catholic religious order — during Venetian rule. The doorway facing you is the giveaway: two columns with Corinthian-style capitals, a carved frame and a circular skylight above, all in the restrained, learned style of the Italian Renaissance. The design is thought to follow a pattern by Sebastiano Serlio, the same Italian architect whose books shaped the Rimondi Fountain. So this was a Renaissance church first.

In 1646 the Ottomans took Rethymno, and the church became a mosque, renamed for Gazi Hüseyin Pasha, the commander who had captured the city. The building kept its Christian doorway and gained the things a mosque needs: a mihrab, the niche that shows the direction of Mecca, and a minaret, the tower from which a muezzin calls the faithful to prayer. The minaret here is late — 1890, near the end of Ottoman rule — and it was built by an engineer with a thoroughly Greek name, Georgios Daskalakis. Sit with that for a second. In the last decades of Ottoman Crete, a Greek Christian could still be the man hired to build a mosque's minaret. This was not two peoples in two sealed boxes; it was a mixed, unequal, complicated society, and the buildings show it.

The third life began in the 1920s. After the Greco-Turkish war, Greece and Turkey agreed in 1923 to exchange their minorities by religion — a treaty that uprooted about a million and a half people. Crete's Muslims, most of them Cretan-born and Greek-speaking, left the island in 1924. The mosque was left standing and empty, and the town turned it into a music school. That is what it still is: the Municipal Odeon, where Rethymno's children learn instruments. A mosque with a conservatoire inside it, and the tallest thing in town is still its minaret.

Look up and count the minaret's two balconies. The name Neratze is usually explained as coming from the Turkish word for bitter orange, narenciye — a tree that once grew here. Entry from the square is free, but the interior is a working school, so step in only for a concert or when it is openly open. Then head uphill towards the great fortress on the hill.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to look from the square. Concerts inside are ticketed; the interior is a working music school, not a museum.
stops.openingHours: The square is open at all hours. The building opens for concerts and school use, so check locally if you want to see inside.
stops.accessibility: The square in front is level and step-free. The interior has steps at the entrance.
stops.insiderTip: Find the Renaissance doorway on the former church — Corinthian-style columns and a circular skylight — and then look up at the 1890 minaret. Church and mosque in one building, and a music school inside both.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk west and then north through the lanes, climbing gently towards the hill of the Fortezza. Follow the brown tourist signs for 'Fortezza'; after about ten minutes the walls and the main gate come into view, with steps up to the entrance.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Dietmar Rabich, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: The Fortezza
stops.narration:
Climb slowly, because you are walking up the reason for the whole town. This hill is Paleokastro — 'old castle' — and it was almost certainly the acropolis of ancient Rhithymna, the city that stood here long before Venice. An acropolis is the fortified high point of a Greek city, and from up here you can see exactly why: it commands the harbour and the coastal road in both directions.

The fortress you are standing in was a response to a disaster. In 1571 an Ottoman fleet under Uluç Ali Reis — an Italian renegade who had been captured, converted to Islam and risen to become an Ottoman admiral and Pasha of Algiers — attacked Rethymno with some forty galleys and levelled the town. The Venetians had left only a token guard, and the weak walls of 1540 gave way. The lesson was taken: Venice needed a proper citadel. Building began on 13 September 1573 to designs by the military engineer Sforza Pallavicini, in the new bastioned style — angled walls and projecting gun platforms, so that cannonballs glanced off instead of smashing through. It was a colossal job: records say 107,142 Cretans were conscripted for the labour and 40,205 pack animals requisitioned, under a Cretan master builder, Giannis Skordilis. The walls were finished by 1580 and run for about 1,300 metres around the hill.

Here is the uncomfortable part. The Fortezza was meant to shelter the whole city, but it was too small — Rethymno already had more than 5,000 people by 1582 — and it was never finished to its own design. It had no ditch and no outer defences, and the walls were low. A Venetian report of 1602 said it could be scaled with ladders. So when the Ottomans finally came, in the war that would take all of Crete, the fortress did not save the town. On 11 October 1646 the Ottoman army arrived; the city fell on 20 October; the survivors fled up here into a crowded, plague-ridden fort with no ammunition. The commander, Luigi Minotto, held out three weeks and surrendered on 10 November; the castle changed hands on the 13th. Seven years of building and six decades of standing bought the town roughly a month.

Under Ottoman rule the Venetian cathedral inside became the Mosque of Sultan Ibrahim, and houses filled the enclosure. By the twentieth century the Fortezza was a residential quarter and then a prison; after the Second World War the houses were cleared away, leaving the walls and a handful of buildings, and since the 1990s it has been under restoration. Walk the ramparts: the four demi-bastions are named for saints — Nicolas, Paul, Elias and Lucas — and the Erofili open-air theatre, built into the St Elias bastion in 1993, still hosts summer concerts. The Archaeological Museum sits in the Ottoman ravelin, the outwork, by the gate.

Entry is around €5, and hours are typically roughly 08:00 to 20:00 in summer, shorter out of season — verify at the gate, because they change. The interior is rough cobbles and uneven ground with almost no shade, so bring water. When you have had the view, come back down through the lanes to the old city gate.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Around €5 for adults, with reduced rates for children and students; some nationalities and EU youth may qualify for discounts. Prices and seasonal hours move — verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Typically open daily, roughly 08:00–20:00 in summer and shorter in winter, sometimes closing on public holidays. Verify on the day.
stops.accessibility: Honestly difficult. The approach is a cobbled ramp and steps; the interior is rough, uneven ground over a large site with little shade. The gate and main path are manageable, but the full circuit is not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Walk right round the ramparts, not just the central courtyard — the views over the town, the harbour and the coast are the real prize, and the four saint-named bastions each give a different angle. Bring water; there is almost no shade.
stops.nextStopDirections: Come back down from the Fortezza and follow the lanes south into the old town for about ten minutes, heading for the Great Gate and the square beside it. The stone arch of the Porta Guora stands at the end of the street, with a mosque minaret just beyond it.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Dietmar Rabich, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Porta Guora & the Old Lanes
stops.narration:
This is the Megali Porta, the Great Gate — the last real survivor of the walls that once ringed Rethymno. The fortifications went up between 1540 and 1570 to plans by Michele Sanmicheli, the same engineer credited with the Loggia, and this was the town's main landward entrance. It is named after a Rector of Rethymno, J. Guoro. Originally the arch carried a triangular pediment with the lion of Saint Mark, the winged symbol of Venice, carved in relief — a reminder that this was an outpost of a republic whose heart was a lagoon a thousand kilometres away. The walls themselves are gone: under Ottoman rule, and after it, the town simply grew out through them and the stone was pulled down and reused for houses. The gate survived by becoming a passage rather than a defence.

Stand in it and read the Ottoman layer of the town. Right beside the gate is the Valide Sultan Mosque, built in 1670 and named for the mother of Sultan Ibrahim; its minaret went up in 1878. Under Ottoman rule — the Turks called the town Resmo — the lanes filled with a different architecture: timber-framed houses whose upper storeys project over the street on wooden brackets, walls of rubble and mud called bagdati, thickly plastered, and lattice screens, kafasoto, over the windows. You will walk past that mix of Venetian stone and Ottoman wood all the way back to the water.

One last thing belongs to this town, though you will not see it today. Twenty-three kilometres inland stands the monastery of Arkadi. In November 1866, during the Cretan revolt against Ottoman rule, some 943 people — mostly women and children — took refuge there behind its walls. When the besieging Ottoman force broke in, the defenders detonated the gunpowder stored inside rather than surrender; around 846 of those sheltering died, along with many attackers, and the abbot, Gabriel, was among the dead. The 'Holocaust of Arkadi', as it became known, horrified Europe, won the Cretan cause famous sympathisers from Victor Hugo to Garibaldi, and is commemorated here every 8 November. It is the story Cretans tell when they explain who they are.

You are near the end now. The lanes run back down to the harbour from here, the tavernas fill up after dark, the raki — tsikoudia, the clear grape spirit Cretans drink ice-cold — comes out after the meal, and the town settles into its evening. Sit down somewhere and let it.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. The gate and the lanes are public streets, not a ticketed site. Dinner and drinks are at normal restaurant prices.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. The lanes and tavernas are at their best from late afternoon into the night.
stops.accessibility: The gate is a level passage, but the surrounding old-town lanes are narrow, cobbled and uneven, with occasional steps. Take it slowly.
stops.insiderTip: Stand under the arch and look for the ghost of the lion of Saint Mark that once crowned it. Then walk one lane back from the waterfront for dinner — same food, better prices, fewer people than the harbour front.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is the end of the walk. From the gate the lanes run back down to the harbour in a few minutes — pick a taverna, order mezedes to share and whatever fish is on the board, and finish with a small glass of tsikoudia, the local grape spirit that usually arrives on the house. When you are ready to move on, the seasonal fast catamaran to Santorini leaves from Rethymno's port just below the old town: roughly two and a quarter hours, May to October, about twice a week, from around €104 — book ahead and check it is running, because it is seasonal. If it is not sailing, the plan B is a bus to Heraklion (about an hour and a half) and a ferry from Heraklion's port instead. Kali synecheia — good continuation.
